C117 (early-season) · Oaks · team-update · Wilson Shepard (Coach): The Oaks are winning games after halftime, and they have done it since the first game in franchise history. Against Charlotte at home in game one, in front of a sold-out crowd, they trailed 36-32 at the half and 60-49 after three, then scored 36 in the fourth and held the Hornets to 22 to win 85-82. In Detroit they trailed 43-37 at the half and won the second half 54-35 for a 91-78 win. At Golden State they trailed 59-44 at the half, the biggest halftime deficit they have come back from, then won the third 30-19 and the fourth 24-18, outscoring the Warriors 54-37 after the break to win 98-96. In Philadelphia they trailed 82-80 going into the fourth, scored 40 and held the 76ers to 24 for a 120-106 win. In Denver in C116 they were already up 23 after three and still put up 42 in the fourth of a franchise-record 147-114 win. Even the Indiana loss showed it. Down 61-42 at the half and 82-62 after three, the Oaks scored 38 in the fourth, won the quarter 38-22 and came within four, 104-100. Through 13 games the Oaks have won the fourth quarter 10 times, lost it twice and tied it once. One of the two losses was the Orlando game, which was already decided at 101-76 after three. The other was the home loss to San Antonio, tied 90-90 going into the fourth before the Spurs won the quarter by 9. Wilson Shepard's young team finishes. In Indiana a 19-point halftime hole was too much. C117 (early-season) · Oaks · player-feature · Austin Reaves (SG): Austin Reaves is the highest-paid player on the Oaks at $30 million a year, and this cycle he played like it. He led the Oaks in scoring in both games of C117. Against Denver at home he scored 32 in just 22 minutes on 8 of 14, 6 of 10 from three and 10 of 10 at the line, without a turnover. Then at Golden State he had 23 points, 6 rebounds, 5 assists and 3 steals in 33 minutes as the Oaks came back from 15 down at the half to win 98-96. Through 13 games he has led the Oaks in scoring or shared the lead six times: 23 in New York, tied with AJ Dybantsa; 23 in Washington and 19 in Indiana, tied with Adash Stanley; 20 in Toronto; 32 against Denver; and 23 at Golden State. He does it without needing the ball to himself. In the first game in franchise history, the 85-82 home win over Charlotte, he had 20 points and 9 rebounds on 6 of 12, 4 of 9 from three and 4 of 4 at the line without a turnover. He handed out 10 assists in Detroit, had 9 rebounds and 3 steals with his 23 in New York, and in the 147-114 franchise-record win in Denver he scored 27 on 11 of 14, a perfect 5 of 5 from three, with 12 assists. He also answers his bad nights. After going 4 of 14 in Philadelphia he scored 27 in Denver, and after 13 points and 4 turnovers in the home loss to San Antonio he scored 32 against Denver. Jerome (PG), Elliot Abraham (GM): Ten games into their first season, the Oakland Oaks are the number one team in the NBA.com power rankings, ranked first of all 31 teams, and holding the top spot from the week before. The rankings are built on season record and recent form, and the Oaks had both: 9-1 when they came out, 3-0 over the last week, 6-1 over the last two weeks. They earned it against real opponents. Four of the teams in the top nine are teams the Oaks have already beaten: Detroit, ranked 3rd, beaten 91-78 on the road; Oklahoma City, ranked 4th, beaten 101-95 in the Cup opener at home; New York, ranked 6th, beaten 115-93 on the road; and Philadelphia, ranked 8th, beaten 120-106 on the road after trailing by two going into the fourth. Ranked 2nd was San Antonio. The rankings only update once a week, and these came out a game behind. Since then the Spurs came into Oakland for a Cup game and won 126-117, handing the Oaks their first ever home loss. So number one is now 9-2, number two is 8-2, and the gap at the top is half a game. For an expansion team that went 0-9 through rookie camp and the preseason, with a first-year head coach and a first-time GM, being ranked first in the league at all is the story. | Stats: Oaks/NBA.com Power Ranking/#1 of 31/no change, Oaks/9-1 at ranking/3-0 last week/6-1 last two weeks/9-1 last month, Oaks/now 9-2 after Spurs loss, Oaks wins over ranked teams/DET #3/OKC #4/NYK #6/PHI #8 | Team record: 9-2 | Streak: L1

C116 (early-season) · Oaks · season-state · Wilson Shepard (Coach), Mike Paulson (President of Operations), Elliot Abraham (GM): Ten cycles ago this page was asking Wilson Shepard for answers. The Oaks went 0-4 in rookie camp and 0-5 in the preseason, 0-9 before they had played a game that counted, and in C109 the media wanted to know why the team was losing and why the full roster had never been on the floor together. Shepard, a first-year head coach who spent the previous season as an offensive assistant in Minnesota, kept saying the same thing. In C107 he said the Oaks would "catch people off guard this year." In C109 he said, "We're still finding our rhythm. The guys are putting in the work, and I'm confident we'll tighten up and be ready for the real deal. We're not getting the results we want, but we're not letting it get us down either." In C110, after the loss to Miami, he said the full team had yet to suit up as one, that opening night would show a team nobody had seen, and that he was not worried. The fans were. Nine games into the real deal, the Oaks are 8-1, have won four straight and are 1-0 in the NBA Cup. They beat Charlotte 85-82 in the franchise's first game, coming back from 11 down after three, won in Detroit, New York and Washington, lost by four in Indiana after coming back from 20 down, then routed Toronto 135-75 and beat Oklahoma City, Orlando and Philadelphia. They are scoring 109.9 a game and allowing 89.6, a margin of more than 20 points a night. The surprise is how they are winning. Shepard came in as the offensive specialist, but the early identity is defense: Charlotte scored 82, Detroit 78, Toronto 75 and Washington 62. He has also found rotation pieces nobody expected, like second-round rookie Harry Hayward, and kept the bench fresh, with nobody playing more than 28 minutes in the Toronto rout. After the opener he laughed that his ears were still ringing, then said the next loss could be a game away and the job was to build on the good and eliminate the bad. The other half of this story is the man above him. Mike Paulson is president of operations for an 8-1 expansion team, with Elliot Abraham running the day-to-day as GM, and he is also the GM of the A's in the middle of an offseason that has already seen Vinnie Keane retire, Carmen Mesa traded to the Phillies, Mark Aitken drawing Angels interest in free agency and Benji Dillon undecided. In C110 fans worried that a first-year coach, a first-time GM and a front office chief busy with a World Series run was too much uncertainty. So far the Oaks have answered that. Then there is Elliot Abraham, the first-time GM who has said almost nothing since C111. That cycle, with the team 0-9, he told the media nobody was panicking, that the losing was intentional and that every variation they tried was data for the long term. He also said the Draymond Green trade "wasn't ideal form" for a player the community reveres, and that Jerami Grant's status was a matter the league was looking into. In C112 Elias Varek confirmed Grant had failed his medical and credited Paulson and Abraham with building a quality team in one offseason. Abraham has not spoken since. His path here is not a typical basketball one: born in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, adopted young by an American family, MIT, the man who built the first successful professional pickleball league, then senior operations under Varek at Civis Systems and Paulson's day-to-day operator in his one season with the Chicago Bulls before Oakland hired him in C101. The Bulls beat his Oaks in the preseason in C110. He lives in Jack London, has been seen staying late in the clubhouse after wins, and around the waterfront he is still more of a familiar face than a public one. | Stats: Oaks/8-1/W4/109.9 PPG/89.6 OPP PPG/+20.3 margin, Oaks/0-4 rookie camp/0-5 preseason, Oaks/1-0 NBA Cup, Opponents held under 85/CHA 82/DET 78/TOR 75/WAS 62 | Team record: 8-1 | Streak: W4

C116 (early-season) · Oaks · season-state · Wilson Shepard (Coach), Mike Paulson (President of Operations), Elliot Abraham (GM): Ten cycles ago this page was asking Wilson Shepard for answers. The Oaks went 0-4 in rookie camp and 0-5 in the preseason, 0-9 before they had played a game that counted, and in C109 the media wanted to know why the team was losing and why the full roster had never been on the floor together. Shepard, a first-year head coach who spent the previous season as an offensive assistant in Minnesota, kept saying the same thing. In C107 he said the Oaks would "catch people off guard this year." In C109 he said, "We're still finding our rhythm. The guys are putting in the work, and I'm confident we'll tighten up and be ready for the real deal. We're not getting the results we want, but we're not letting it get us down either." In C110, after the loss to Miami, he said the full team had yet to suit up as one, that opening night would show a team nobody had seen, and that he was not worried. The fans were. Nine games into the real deal, the Oaks are 8-1, have won four straight and are 1-0 in the NBA Cup. They beat Charlotte 85-82 in the franchise's first game, coming back from 11 down after three, won in Detroit, New York and Washington, lost by four in Indiana after coming back from 20 down, then routed Toronto 135-75 and beat Oklahoma City, Orlando and Philadelphia. They are scoring 109.9 a game and allowing 89.6, a margin of more than 20 points a night. The surprise is how they are winning. Shepard came in as the offensive specialist, but the early identity is defense: Charlotte scored 82, Detroit 78, Toronto 75 and Washington 62. He has also found rotation pieces nobody expected, like second-round rookie Harry Hayward, and kept the bench fresh, with nobody playing more than 28 minutes in the Toronto rout. After the opener he laughed that his ears were still ringing, then said the next loss could be a game away and the job was to build on the good and eliminate the bad. The other half of this story is the man above him. Mike Paulson is president of operations for an 8-1 expansion team, with Elliot Abraham running the day-to-day as GM, and he is also the GM of the A's in the middle of an offseason that has already seen Vinnie Keane retire, Carmen Mesa traded to the Phillies, Mark Aitken drawing Angels interest in free agency and Benji Dillon undecided. In C110 fans worried that a first-year coach, a first-time GM and a front office chief busy with a World Series run was too much uncertainty. So far the Oaks have answered that. Then there is Elliot Abraham, the first-time GM who has said almost nothing since C111. That cycle, with the team 0-9, he told the media nobody was panicking, that the losing was intentional and that every variation they tried was data for the long term. He also said the Draymond Green trade "wasn't ideal form" for a player the community reveres, and that Jerami Grant's status was a matter the league was looking into. In C112 Elias Varek confirmed Grant had failed his medical and credited Paulson and Abraham with building a quality team in one offseason. Abraham has not spoken since. His path here is not a typical basketball one: born in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, adopted young by an American family, MIT, the man who built the first successful professional pickleball league, then senior operations under Varek at Civis Systems and Paulson's day-to-day operator in his one season with the Chicago Bulls before Oakland hired him in C101. The Bulls beat his Oaks in the preseason in C110. He lives in Jack London, has been seen staying late in the clubhouse after wins, and around the waterfront he is still more of a familiar face than a public one. | Stats: Oaks/8-1/W4/109.9 PPG/89.6 OPP PPG/+20.3 margin, Oaks/0-4 rookie camp/0-5 preseason, Oaks/1-0 NBA Cup, Opponents held under 85/CHA 82/DET 78/TOR 75/WAS 62 | Team record: 8-1 | Streak: W4

C116 (early-season) · Oaks · season-state · Wilson Shepard (Coach), Mike Paulson (President of Operations), Elliot Abraham (GM): Ten cycles ago this page was asking Wilson Shepard for answers. The Oaks went 0-4 in rookie camp and 0-5 in the preseason, 0-9 before they had played a game that counted, and in C109 the media wanted to know why the team was losing and why the full roster had never been on the floor together. Shepard, a first-year head coach who spent the previous season as an offensive assistant in Minnesota, kept saying the same thing. In C107 he said the Oaks would "catch people off guard this year." In C109 he said, "We're still finding our rhythm. The guys are putting in the work, and I'm confident we'll tighten up and be ready for the real deal. We're not getting the results we want, but we're not letting it get us down either." In C110, after the loss to Miami, he said the full team had yet to suit up as one, that opening night would show a team nobody had seen, and that he was not worried. The fans were. Nine games into the real deal, the Oaks are 8-1, have won four straight and are 1-0 in the NBA Cup. They beat Charlotte 85-82 in the franchise's first game, coming back from 11 down after three, won in Detroit, New York and Washington, lost by four in Indiana after coming back from 20 down, then routed Toronto 135-75 and beat Oklahoma City, Orlando and Philadelphia. They are scoring 109.9 a game and allowing 89.6, a margin of more than 20 points a night. The surprise is how they are winning. Shepard came in as the offensive specialist, but the early identity is defense: Charlotte scored 82, Detroit 78, Toronto 75 and Washington 62. He has also found rotation pieces nobody expected, like second-round rookie Harry Hayward, and kept the bench fresh, with nobody playing more than 28 minutes in the Toronto rout. After the opener he laughed that his ears were still ringing, then said the next loss could be a game away and the job was to build on the good and eliminate the bad. The other half of this story is the man above him. Mike Paulson is president of operations for an 8-1 expansion team, with Elliot Abraham running the day-to-day as GM, and he is also the GM of the A's in the middle of an offseason that has already seen Vinnie Keane retire, Carmen Mesa traded to the Phillies, Mark Aitken drawing Angels interest in free agency and Benji Dillon undecided. In C110 fans worried that a first-year coach, a first-time GM and a front office chief busy with a World Series run was too much uncertainty. So far the Oaks have answered that. Then there is Elliot Abraham, the first-time GM who has said almost nothing since C111. That cycle, with the team 0-9, he told the media nobody was panicking, that the losing was intentional and that every variation they tried was data for the long term. He also said the Draymond Green trade "wasn't ideal form" for a player the community reveres, and that Jerami Grant's status was a matter the league was looking into. In C112 Elias Varek confirmed Grant had failed his medical and credited Paulson and Abraham with building a quality team in one offseason. Abraham has not spoken since. His path here is not a typical basketball one: born in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, adopted young by an American family, MIT, the man who built the first successful professional pickleball league, then senior operations under Varek at Civis Systems and Paulson's day-to-day operator in his one season with the Chicago Bulls before Oakland hired him in C101. The Bulls beat his Oaks in the preseason in C110. He lives in Jack London, has been seen staying late in the clubhouse after wins, and around the waterfront he is still more of a familiar face than a public one. | Stats: Oaks/8-1/W4/109.9 PPG/89.6 OPP PPG/+20.3 margin, Oaks/0-4 rookie camp/0-5 preseason, Oaks/1-0 NBA Cup, Opponents held under 85/CHA 82/DET 78/TOR 75/WAS 62 | Team record: 8-1 | Streak: W4

angleRead.name: Talia Finch
angleRead.text: I want to go back to the same West Oakland room and sit with what the comeback has changed there—and what it has not. The Oaks are 11-2, have won the fourth quarter 10 times in 13 games, and just came back from 15 down at Golden State, the team that left Oakland. I will watch the replay with the regulars, count who stays with it and who turns away, and ask whether this team has become part of their day or only a good score to talk about. I will keep the quiet answer too: the people who do not have to think about the Oaks at all.

plan.focus: The Oaks' comeback identity as it lands in West Oakland: belief, fatigue, indifference, and the distance between winning games and belonging to a neighborhood.
plan.why: Selena has the pattern in the numbers. Mine is the room after the pattern: a team that keeps winning second halves, an expansion franchise now 11-2, and a city still deciding whether that means anything in ordinary life. The same room gives me continuity instead of a single reaction, and the Golden State win adds a specific Oakland charge without requiring me to claim more than I witness.
